sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Cursor confirms security breach led to malicious Claude Code extension

stories.headline: Cursor breach let attackers push fake Claude Code extension
stories.dek: A key stolen from Fireworks AI led to leaked agent traces, stolen credentials and a backdoored extension served to up to 5,000 developers.
stories.body:
Cursor has confirmed a security breach that let attackers publish malicious copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension through its extension marketplace, BleepingComputer reports. The intrusion began with an access key stolen from Fireworks AI, a third-party provider Cursor used for model training and inference. Up to 5,000 developers may have received the tainted builds.

According to Cursor's incident report, published Friday, the attackers used the Fireworks key to copy a read-only storage bucket Cursor shared with the provider. It held historical AI coding-agent traces, mostly from 2025, from users who had not enabled Privacy Mode. Some traces contained unredacted API credentials. Cursor says fewer than 0.05 percent of users had traces exposed and fewer than 0.01 percent had credentials compromised.

Those credentials opened more doors. The attackers took archived, non-production source code repositories, customer support emails, usage metrics, contact details, summaries of some agent conversations, and credentials customers had shared with support. Cursor's monitoring flagged the activity and the company revoked the key and rotated credentials. By then, the attackers already held a credential for its marketplace.

On October 29 they placed malicious versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 of the extension directly on the cache serving Cursor's VS Code marketplace. The builds were live for about 11 hours. They ran JavaScript that collected system information, installed an attacker-controlled SSH key, tried to enable SSH and set up persistence. Security researchers found coding errors that likely broke the backdoor on many Windows and macOS machines where SSH was not already on. Anthropic's legitimate extension and Open VSX were not compromised.

Cursor says production infrastructure, official app releases, customer code repositories and Privacy Mode data were untouched. It has moved all inference traffic off Fireworks, rebuilt its marketplace and redeployed production as a precaution. Users who installed or updated the extension during the window should follow its remediation guidance.

The breach is part of what Wiz calls "Black October," a wave of attacks on AI developer platforms aimed at credentials for AI models. Railway, Northflank, Lightning AI, OpenCode and Warp were hit. At Railway, stolen secrets generated about $740,000 in fraudulent AI charges. Fireworks itself disclosed multiple breaches in October, which also exposed some Notion AI chat transcripts.
key_points: Attackers used a Fireworks AI key to reach Cursor's shared data bucket
Agent traces held unredacted credentials that unlocked more Cursor systems
Malicious Claude Code versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 live for about 11 hours
Up to 5,000 developers may have received an SSH backdoor
stories.why_it_matters: If you use Cursor and touched the Claude Code extension around October 29, check for unknown SSH keys and follow Cursor's remediation steps. More broadly, agent traces can leak secrets, so keep credentials out of prompts and consider Privacy Mode.

cover.caption: Developers who may have received the backdoored extension

sources.name: Hacker News
sources.title: Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages

stories.headline: Lovable apps leak passport data and 200,000 private messages
stories.dek: Researchers scanned 159,041 projects built on the Swedish AI app builder and found personal data readable without logging in.
stories.body:
Web apps built with Lovable, the Stockholm-based AI app builder, are exposing sensitive personal data to anyone who knows where to look. That is the finding of researchers at Crissy Field, who examined 159,041 Lovable projects in collaboration with German business daily Handelsblatt. The exposed data includes passport numbers and more than 200,000 private chat messages.

The researchers used Common Crawl web archive data to find Lovable projects from December 2025 to September 2026. Of those, 34,545 used the Supabase database service, and 24,664 sent database records as soon as the page loaded, with no login. That alone is not necessarily a problem, since some data is meant to be public. But further read-only requests using the same API key returned more. The team found email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403 of those 24,664 sites, or 30 percent.

The researchers caution that the 30 percent figure is not a confirmed leak rate. Some addresses may be public contacts or test data, and the sample is not representative of all Lovable apps. Specific cases are harder to dismiss. A German lifestyle forum exposed more than 80,000 profiles with names, birth dates and gender, plus over 200,000 chat messages. A service provider exposed more than 1,000 records with passport numbers, expiration dates and nationalities. Event organizers and restaurants exposed ticket and payment records, and one provider left 280,000 customer emails accessible.

The researchers say they could not establish whether any data had been misused. They are not publishing how to access it. Handelsblatt contacted Lovable with the findings.

The report points to a gap between marketing and fine print. Lovable promotes building apps with no technical knowledge, but its terms place responsibility for applications and data handling on customers. Because Lovable's database integrations follow recurring patterns, the researchers warn, an attack that works on one app may work on many others with little extra effort. Lovable's own database features, introduced in late 2025, were not examined.
key_points: Researchers examined 159,041 Lovable projects, 34,545 using Supabase
Email-containing tables found on 7,403 of 24,664 sites, or 30 percent
Over 1,000 passport records and 200,000 chat messages exposed
Lovable's terms make customers responsible for app security
stories.why_it_matters: AI-generated apps can ship with misconfigured database access that non-developers will not spot, and repeated patterns make mass scanning easy. Anyone building on Lovable and Supabase should audit access rules before handling real user data.

cover.caption: Private chat messages exposed by one Lovable-built forum

stories.body:
SpaceX says it caught Starship at the end of Flight 15, according to the company's launch page for the mission, published on November 14.

The announcement is brief: SpaceX reports that the catch ended the flight. The company has not yet detailed the mission profile, the timeline or how the vehicle performed during the flight.

The news drew wide attention among developers and engineers online and became one of the day's most discussed tech stories.

Further details on the flight are expected to come from SpaceX.

Announcement posted on SpaceX's launch page on November 14
Mission details not yet published by the company
stories.why_it_matters: A catch at the end of a flight points toward reusable heavy-lift hardware, which could change launch cadence and costs for the satellite and space industry.

sources.name: Tom's Hardware
sources.title: U.S. Treasury Secretary questions whether Nvidia knowingly sold AI GPUs to shell companies, says company itself is responsible

stories.headline: Bessent says Nvidia must answer for AI GPUs sold to shell companies
stories.dek: The Treasury Secretary questions Nvidia's internal controls and criticizes its general counsel, but says it is unclear whether Jensen Huang knew.
stories.body:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Nvidia should be held accountable if restricted AI GPUs reached China through shell companies, Tom's Hardware reports. In a CNBC interview, he said the real question is whether Nvidia knew its clients. "If this was happening, then there were not robust controls at the company," Bessent said, adding, "We do not know for a fact that Jensen Huang knew this."

Bessent criticized general counsel Timothy Teter, who reportedly asked the Commerce Department whether U.S. authorities were behind the detention of Megaspeed's Alice Wong in Singapore. He said he expects Nvidia's board to investigate thoroughly.

He admitted there is "a lot of leakage" in export controls, but called for enforcing existing rules rather than adding new ones. Treasury, War, State and USTR backed blacklisting Megaspeed for months, he said. Commerce's BIS reportedly stalled the move over China trade tensions.
key_points: Bessent says Nvidia, not just Jensen Huang, is responsible for whether restricted GPUs reached shell companies.
He criticized Nvidia general counsel Timothy Teter over inquiries to the Commerce Department about Megaspeed's Alice Wong.
Bessent says several agencies backed adding Megaspeed to the Entity List for months; Commerce's BIS reportedly stalled it.

sources.name: Bloomberg
sources.title: White House AI task force urges agencies to ease liability to encourage incident reporting

stories.headline: White House AI task force urges agencies to ease cyber liability
stories.dek: Officials want looser liability policies so AI companies will report critical incidents instead of staying quiet, Bloomberg reports.
stories.body:
The White House AI task force has told federal agencies to relax cyber liability policies to encourage AI companies to report critical incidents, according to Bloomberg. The message came at a closed-door meeting at the White House.

Task force officials argued that older enforcement standards may be outdated and could discourage companies from sharing information, Bloomberg reports. The idea is that firms facing less legal exposure would be more willing to disclose when something goes seriously wrong with their AI systems.

Bloomberg did not detail which agencies attended the meeting or which specific policies would change. The guidance points to an approach that favors voluntary disclosure by AI developers over strict penalties.
key_points: Bloomberg reports the White House AI task force told agencies to relax cyber liability policies.
The aim is to get AI companies to report critical incidents.
Officials argued older enforcement standards may be outdated and discourage information sharing.

sources.name: Hacker News
sources.title: Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities 90 days after reporting

stories.headline: Project Zero drops patch grace periods, moves to fixed 90-day disclosure
stories.dek: Google's bug hunters will publish flaws on a fixed clock regardless of fix status, shrinking to 60 days in February and 30 days in 2028.
stories.body:
Google Project Zero is replacing its "90 + 30" disclosure policy with "Full 90": vulnerabilities will be disclosed 90 days after they are reported to the vendor, whether or not a patch has shipped. The deadline drops to 60 days on February 2, 2027, and to 30 days on January 3, 2028. Grace periods and variant rules are gone. Exceptions remain for bugs exploited in the wild, bugs already made public, and vendor requests.

The team blames AI. It says LLMs let attackers find bugs faster and reverse engineer patches almost immediately, which makes the old 30-day "soak time" meaningless. Project Zero says it now finds several vulnerabilities a week in targets that once yielded a few a year.

It will still track whether bugs are fixed, but fix status will no longer affect the disclosure date.
key_points: Project Zero now discloses bugs 90 days after reporting, dropping to 60 days on Feb. 2, 2027 and 30 days on Jan. 3, 2028.
Grace periods and the 30-day patch soak time are removed; exceptions cover in-the-wild exploits, public bugs and vendor requests.
Project Zero cites LLM-driven bug discovery and fast patch reverse engineering as the reason for the change.

sources.name: Hacker News
sources.title: Nvidia deliberately kept GPU prices high through circular financing deals

stories.headline: Report alleges Nvidia used customer financing to keep GPU prices high
stories.dek: TechSpot, citing a Wall Street Journal profile of interim CEO Colette Kress, says the deals helped absorb surplus TSMC wafers.
stories.body:
Nvidia pushed for more financing deals with its own customers in mid-to-late 2026 to absorb an oversupply of TSMC wafers and keep GPU prices high, according to a Wall Street Journal profile of interim CEO Colette Kress. TechSpot goes further, arguing that high prices were the aim of former CEO Jensen Huang's strategy. Nvidia has long faced accusations of circular financing, and Huang and Kress have rejected comparisons to Enron.

According to the report, Kress privately worried about the scale of deals with cloud providers and AI companies such as OpenAI. By summer 2026, facing an "avalanche" of chips ordered from TSMC, Nvidia slowed, downsized or paused some deals. One with OpenAI originally included a $250 billion backstop for a data center.

TechSpot says GeForce cards often sell for more than 160 percent of MSRP. Huang resigned after revelations of extramarital affairs.
key_points: The Wall Street Journal reports Nvidia sought more customer financing deals in mid-to-late 2026 to absorb surplus TSMC wafers and keep GPU prices high.
Nvidia later slowed or paused some deals, including an OpenAI arrangement that originally included a $250 billion backstop.
TechSpot says GeForce GPUs often sell for more than 160 percent of MSRP.

opinion.headline: If the AI wrote the app, the platform owns the defaults
opinion.dek: AI app builders that sell to people who cannot read code should ship locked-down apps and stop pushing security onto customers through fine print.
opinion.body:
A service provider that built its app with Lovable left more than 1,000 records open to the internet, complete with passport numbers, expiration dates and nationalities. No login was needed. A German lifestyle forum built the same way exposed more than 80,000 profiles and over 200,000 private chat messages. Event organizers and restaurants exposed ticket and payment records, and one provider left 280,000 customer emails accessible. These cases come from researchers at Crissy Field, who examined 159,041 projects built on the Stockholm-based AI app builder in collaboration with German business daily Handelsblatt, in findings shared on Hacker News.

The same researchers point to a gap between marketing and fine print. Lovable promotes building apps with no technical knowledge. Its terms place responsibility for applications and data handling on customers. Put those two sentences next to each other and the deal is clear: the platform's AI writes code for people who cannot read it, then the platform hands those people the job of securing it. That is a product sold with none of the liability kept. AI app builders should own secure defaults. Telling non-developers to audit their own database rules is the admin:admin password of this era.

The numbers deserve care. Of the 159,041 projects, 34,545 used the Supabase database service, and 24,664 sent database records as soon as the page loaded, with no login. That is not necessarily a problem, since some records are meant to be public. But further read-only requests with the same API key returned more. The team found email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403 of those 24,664 sites, or 30 percent. The researchers caution that this is not a confirmed leak rate. Some addresses may be public contacts or test entries, the sample is not representative of all Lovable apps, and Lovable's own database features, introduced in late 2025, were not examined. Nor could the team establish that anything had been misused.

Lovable is not alone. Ars Technica reports that security firm Claroc found a design flaw in Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, that lets anyone enumerate thousands of live share links. Except in rare cases, opening a link reveals all of an app's data: business plans, medical exam results, employee names and ID numbers. Claroc says 35,578 of the 37,571 Grok-built apps it found online were open without a sign-in, according to The Hacker News. Among the exposed projects were 24 apps built by SpaceXSI itself, showing a confidential onboarding plan and a sales territory map of 594 accounts. If the company that makes the tool cannot keep its own apps closed, what chance does a restaurant owner have? After Ars Technica sent questions, SpaceXSI pulled its own 24 apps. Most other exposed data stayed online.

There is an old name for this pattern. The Hacker News reports that a default admin:admin password let two researchers take over the login systems behind two car brands' mobile apps and access any customer's account. Nobody reading that blames the drivers. A default credential is the vendor's failure, because the vendor chose it and the buyer never saw it. An AI-generated app that answers database requests from strangers is the same failure with a friendlier interface.

The strongest objection is that a platform is a tool, and only the customer knows what an app is for. The researchers themselves say that serving records without a login is not automatically a flaw, and that 30 percent is not a leak rate. A builder cannot guess which table is meant to be public and which holds passport numbers. And no misuse has been shown. All fair. But the objection assumes a customer who can check, and the sales pitch is aimed at exactly the customer who cannot. Intent is a plain-language question the builder can ask before it publishes anything. The default is the one thing the platform fully controls. Closed until the customer says otherwise costs one extra question. Open until the customer learns database rules exposes passport numbers.

Scale settles the argument. Because Lovable's database integrations follow recurring patterns, the researchers warn, an attack that works on one app may work on many others with little extra effort. A mistake repeated across thousands of apps is not thousands of customer errors. It is one product decision.

Anyone building on Lovable and Supabase should audit access rules before handling real user data, or ask someone who can. Then watch two things. Handelsblatt has contacted Lovable with the findings, and the response that matters is a change to defaults or terms, not a statement. Claroc says its notice to SpaceXSI got no response, so watch whether the remaining Grok Build apps get closed. My prediction, and it is only that: the first confirmed case of misuse will make the fine print look much thinner than these companies hope.
opinion.pull_quote: Telling non-developers to audit their own database rules is the admin:admin password of this era.
opinion.topic: AI app builders and insecure defaults
opinion.thesis: When Lovable's terms make customers responsible for securing apps that its AI wrote for people who can't read the code, the platform has sold a product and kept none of the liability. AI app builders should own secure defaults, as Grok Build's enumerable share links and 30 percent of scanned Lovable sites leaking email tables show. Telling non-developers to audit their own database rules is the admin:admin password of this era.
